new_statements.relation_note: The language has no catalog record and no existing stress statement; this is the first statement found. It supplies a (hedged) weight-sensitive rule: antepenult default with penult attraction by a long penult, and final stress in all-short disyllables, credited to Pentland 1979a and checked against the Jefferson and Heckewelder accent marks. The author repeatedly warns the exact rules are not recoverable.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tested against the accent marks and syncope patterns in the Jefferson and Heckewelder word lists, Pentland's (1979a) rules hold in most cases: disyllables are stressed on the penult, but on the final syllable when both vowels are short; words of three or more syllables are stressed on the antepenult, unless the antepenult is short and the penult long, in which case the penult is stressed. Stress is assigned before apocope and syncope (so an antepenult stressed at the pre-apocope stage may surface as a penult or final, and unstressed schwa/i syncopate). Cunningham adds that the corpus is too small and dialectally mixed for firm rules: p. 45 'it does not present any new data on the rules governing stress in the language.. Pentland (1979a) concluded that deriving regular stress rules would be impossible'; p. 167 'Pentland (1979a, p. 318) notes that there is no clear unified stress pattern in Heckewelder, though disyllabic words tend to be stressed on the penult'; p. 288 'the lack of a uniform pattern for stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Jefferson <màt_ta> 'no' and Heckewelder <máttit> stressed on the first syllable although both vowels are short (p. 126); <wi_lèn_[n]o>/<Wilánno> 'tongue' with penult stress despite a short penult and long antepenult (pp. 128, 170); <Mángeiju> 'large' with antepenult stress despite a short antepenult and long penult (p. 168); <Huppunĕiju> 'north' possibly showing an inherently stressed directional suffix *-ēyǝw (p. 170); copyist disagreements between Heckewelder and Duponceau on <Kíke>/<Kiké> 'life' and <Wéchsiki>/<Wechsíki> 'husband' (pp. 167-168); Pentland's exceptions <Mist.> 'foot', <n'Daan> 'daughter', <Wichtóney> 'beard' where a short vowel is syncopated instead of stressed or stress sits on a short vowel next to a long one (p. 169); aphaeresis in <spummend> 'heaven'/<Schpummend> 'high' contrary to the antepenult rule (pp. 170-171). Cunningham attributes the irregularity to the lists recording coalesced speech of several groups plus idiolectal syncope variation (p. 171).
new_statements.identity_note: Cunningham 2023 treats Nanticoke as 'the Eastern dialect continuum of Maryland Algonquian' recorded in three 18th-century lists: Murray 1792 (Choptank, ch. 4; no accent marks apart from Murray's '!'), the Jefferson manuscript (ch. 5) and Heckewelder's 1785 lists as copied by Heckewelder and Duponceau (ch. 6). All stress evidence comes from the Jefferson and Heckewelder lists, which the author says record the coalesced speech of several groups ('l', 'y' and 't' dialects). The rules themselves are Pentland's (1979a), formulated on the aggregated lists and modelled on Narragansett.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources: the works read in the first reading (Brinton 1893, Speck 1915, Wikipedia) say nothing about stress placement, and the one substantive source, Cunningham 2023, reports Pentland's (1979a) rules as largely corroborated. Within Cunningham 2023 there is internal tension: the stress sections say the examples 'corroborate' and 'neatly corroborate' Pentland's weight-sensitive rules, while the limitations (p. 45), the end of 6.4 (p. 171) and the conclusion (p. 288) say the exact rules are not recoverable and that there is no uniform stress pattern; two copyists (Heckewelder vs Duponceau) also mark different syllables on 'life' and 'husband'. The unopened academia.edu paper (work 1) could not be checked.

sources.note: The only descriptive source Glottolog lists (listed by Glottolog as a phonology) and the only modern phonological analysis of the language; a 425-page phonology built from the Murray and Heckewelder vocabularies is the one place a Nanticoke stress statement (or a statement that stress is unrecoverable) would be made. Wikipedia's phonology section is drawn from it.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ethnography of the Delaware community; no Nanticoke-language data beyond citing Murray/Brinton; the phrase 'with a rising accent' (p. 42-43) refers to an English greeting, not Nanticoke.

Tertiary. Phonology section (consonants, vowels, /l/~[r] word-finally) cites Cunningham 2023/2024 dissertation and gives its direct PDF URL; repeats Murray's '!' = 'peculiar, forcible, explosive, enunciation' of a syllable; no statement on word stress placement.

sources.citation: Brinton, Daniel G. 1893. A Vocabulary of the Nanticoke Dialect. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 31(142): 325-333 (prints William Vans Murray's 1792 vocabulary with Murray's covering letter to Jefferson)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress rule. The only prosodic remark is Brinton's note on p. 327: 'The exclamation point, !, so frequently introduced by Mr. Murray, he explains to signify a peculiar, forcible, explosive enunciation of the syllable.' (e.g. 'Bread, app!ow', 'Belly, nut-ah !', 'Chesnut-tree, eh !qua-mintz'). The '!' is not analysed as stress by Brinton.
